title: Running to Egypt for Help
overview: Isaiah warns Judah that seeking Egypt's protection against Assyria will end in shame, yet promises that God still wants to be kind to them and will bring Assyria down.

parts.label: A useless deal with Egypt (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: Judah's leaders sent envoys to Egyptian royal cities, with costly gifts carried across a dangerous desert, to buy protection from the Assyrian empire without asking the LORD. God gives Egypt the nickname Rahab, an old name for a sea monster, and adds that it sits idle: a great power that talks big and then does nothing.

parts.label: People who want pleasant lies (vv. 8-14)
parts.note: Isaiah is told to write the warning down so later readers can see it was given in advance, because the people wanted prophets to tell them only comforting things. Their scheming is pictured as a bulging wall that suddenly collapses and shatters like a clay pot, leaving no piece big enough to carry a coal or scoop water.

parts.label: Quiet trust versus fast horses (vv. 15-17)
parts.note: Safety lay in turning back to God and staying calm, but the people preferred swift war horses, probably cavalry they hoped to get from Egypt. So they will run indeed, beaten so badly that the few survivors stand alone like a single signal pole on a bare hill.

parts.label: God waits to be gracious (vv. 18-26)
parts.note: Despite all this, the LORD promises to answer their cries, guide them like a voice behind them saying "this is the way," and lead them to throw away their silver and gold idols as something unclean. Rain, rich harvests, streams on hilltops and a brighter sun picture a future in which the LORD binds up and heals his people's wounds.

parts.label: Fire falls on Assyria (vv. 27-33)
parts.note: God is pictured arriving like a storm of fire to strike Assyria, while his people sing as they would on a festival night. Topheth was a place outside Jerusalem linked with burning children as sacrifices, and here it becomes a vast fire pit made ready for "the king," usually read as Assyria's king.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the bright promises of verses 18 to 26 were fulfilled in Judah's own history or point to a future still to come.
think: When you feel threatened, what makes it hard to stay calm instead of grabbing the quickest source of help on offer?
